manifest.name: dsh-pause-resume
manifest.description: One header button stops running turns, goals and jobs, writes a plan to disk, and restores that work after a restart or crash; the button shape is the only status.

readme.text:
One button in the DeepSeek Harness session header. It stops what is running — asking a running turn
to wrap up first — writes a small plan to disk, and after a restart the same button puts that work
back.

* ⏸ — work is running. Press to stop it.
* ▶ — work is stopped, or a previous process left work to restore. Press to restore it.
* ↻ — a turn stopped on its own. Press to continue what did not finish.
* ⏸ dimmed — nothing to stop, restore or continue.

The glyph is the only status. There is no counter, no panel, no badge and no toast, because a second
indicator would be a second source of truth for the same fact. When the last press left something for
a person to look at, the one-sentence tooltip says so and the button still offers the same glyph.

| Work | Pause | Restore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A session with an unfinished turn | turn wrapped up or cancelled, session recorded | session mounted, then one visible continuation message |
| A goal that was armed | paused with the revision it had | `goals.resume` with that exact revision; the goal driver continues on its own |
| A session that only carried that goal | recorded, nothing stopped | mounted; the resumed goal takes over |
| A running background job | killed and recorded | recorded only: a job is a live process, not replayable, so the continuation message names it and the turn restarts it if the work still needs it |
| A session that ended normally | untouched | untouched, and never recorded in the first place |
| A terminal / finished session | untouched | untouched |
| A schedule | untouched | untouched |

Schedules are not paused: the schedule service has no disable operation, only delete, and deleting a
person's schedule to pause it is not a trade this plugin makes. A schedule that fires while paused
starts a turn, but the button keeps showing ▶ while a pause plan waits: a pending plan owns the main
action, so the only honest next step is to finish the restore. The schedule appears in that restore
summary like any other work started after the press.

A press does not cancel at once. It first asks the turn that is running to wrap up, and cancels only
what is still running when the window closes: `wrapUpMs` (default 3000; `0` cancels immediately, as
every version before 0.9.0 did). A turn that ends inside the window is stopped as completed; the rest
are cancelled when the time is up, so a pause still never leaves a turn running behind it. Either way
the plan is written and the sessions are recorded, and the next step is the same: press ▶ to restore,
or restart and let the plan be picked up. When something had to be cancelled, the tooltip says the
work to continue is saved; when everything wrapped up by itself, it says nothing extra.

If the window closes with the steer still unread, the press takes it back: a pause that did not happen
must not replay later as a fresh instruction in the restored session. Only that one message is
removed, only for sessions that timed out, and only while it is still queued; when the queue is not
readable the report says `retractUnavailable` instead of claiming a clean queue.

A plan nobody will press again closes itself. After a restart by hand, finishing those sessions
yourself is enough: each stopped turn is seen living on, moved forward and no longer running, so the
plan settles the way a completed restore does and the button returns to pause, with no press. Only
turns the pause itself stopped are considered, and only on positive evidence: a session still working,
a session list that cannot be read, or an error keeps the plan exactly as it was.
A restore is not a claim that work continued. It is three honest steps per item:

1. **Mount.** A stopped session is mounted through the Harness resume path, which preserves its agent
   preset. If it is already mounted, that step is skipped.
2. **Continue, only where the press actually cancelled a turn.** The continuation is one ordinary
   user message sent through `sessionController.prompt`, with a request id derived from the plan and
   the session. The id makes a repeated restore idempotent, and the message is visible in the
   transcript, so the person can see exactly what was resumed.
3. **Re-arm a goal** with the revision it had when paused. The revision is the person's veto: if the
   goal changed while paused, it is not ours to resume and the item is `skipped`.

Every attempt is journaled with the id of the process that made it, but a journal is reporting, not a
promise: the next boot asks the live Harness again instead of trusting an old row. The continuation
request id is derived from the plan and the session, so a retry before a turn starts is deduplicated
by the Host. A failure leaves the plan on disk and the next press retries every item that still needs
work.

A subagent session cannot be mounted by this process: its parent chat owns the routing. That row is
reported once as attention for the parent, not retried as a failure, so it never keeps the plan open.

A press writes a snapshot. A crash writes nothing, so the plugin keeps a heartbeat instead:
`running.json` holds the sessions whose turn is open right now and the id of the process that wrote
it. The previous process's record is turned into a crash plan in `pending.json` before the heartbeat
file is replaced, so a second or third restart still sees the same work and offers ▶ with no press
needed.

A crash record is weaker than a press: it proves a session existed, not that a turn was open after the
restart. Restore attaches every recorded session and reads the live turn. A row whose turn is still
running is continued; a row that is idle is left idle by the probe, which mounts it to read it and does
not prompt it. A row whose state cannot be read or proven is reported as unknown, and unknown is not
finished: the plan stays on disk, the button keeps offering ▶, and the next press tries again. A
recorded goal is restored whether or not its session's turn is provable, because dropping it was the
path that ended a crashed set with every goal in attention and none resumed. Sessions that ended
normally never enter the file.

The same process reloading the plugin (hot reload) sees its own id and knows there is nothing to
restore. A `pausing` plan found on disk means the press itself was interrupted: those sessions are
left alone, and the button keeps offering the restore until a person presses it.

readme.section: Stops that were not a press
readme.text:
A turn can end without a person pressing anything: the provider returns an error after its own
retries, or the model hits its output limit. Those turns are the one case a restart cannot fix on its
own, so the plugin keeps a separate small ledger, `continue.json`, and offers ↻ instead of ▶. The
ledger is independent of the pause plan: it never turns into a crash plan, never pauses or cancels
anything, and never sends a message by itself.

What becomes a candidate:

readme.section: Stops that were not a press
readme.text:
* A session's latest turn ended `error` or `max-tokens`, and no later turn started or ended.
* The session is a root session with no parent and is not a subagent. A child's stop is answered by
  its parent's tool result; continuing the child alone would speak into a conversation nobody reads.
* The turn did not end `completed`, `aborted`, `interrupted` or `blocked`. A manual pause aborts its
  turn, so the stop a person asked for never appears here; a block before admission is work that
  never ran and is left alone.

readme.section: Stops that were not a press
readme.text:
The press continues the rows visible at that moment, two at a time, with an ordinary user message.
It is not a retry loop: a row that fails stays in the ledger for the next press, and the button
returns to ↻ when anything is still waiting. A row disappears when a newer turn starts, when the
session is already open, when the goal is active, when the session is gone, or when the continued
turn completes. Title comes from the session's own title event; nothing is loaded just to name a
row. The batch is capped at 40 rows, and a row keeps its attempt number across failed presses.

readme.section: Stops that were not a press
readme.text:
Each row is labelled for display only: `blocking` when it already needs a person or its error code is
one a retry cannot fix (auth, permission, quota, unknown model, context length), `actionable` otherwise.
`pendingContinue` carries both counts next to `count`, so failed work stays visible while a batch is
running; the label never hides a row and never changes what a press does — one press still continues
every visible row.

readme.section: Stops that were not a press
readme.text:
Starting a new message in a session that has a waiting row is a takeover: it clears that row without
claiming anything about the old work. Work continues only after a press, never on plugin load, never
on a timer, and never because the previous batch failed.

Six long sessions restored at once are six upstream model requests at once, and a gateway that is
happy with one slow stream is often unhappy with six. For Direct API users this is usually fine and
the extra waiting is pure cost, so progressive restore is **off by default**: restore follows the
ordinary path with no added spacing, no request pool and no cooldown timer installed at all.

Turn it on when batch restores run into rate limits or timeouts: a shared account or gateway quota,
a self-hosted proxy with limited capacity, or an environment where restoring several sessions at
once is what triggers the failures. Single-session timeouts are not helped by it; those need
investigation of the request and the upstream.

Two layers, because either alone is enough to defeat the other:

* **Dispatch spacing.** Sessions are restored in waves by lineage depth, with a gap of
  `restoreStartGapMs` (3 s) plus up to 0.4 s jitter between starts.
* **A real request pool.** The plugin registers an `llm/stream` middleware and holds one permit per
  adapter request until that stream ends, fails or is cancelled — not when the turn opens, not when
  the first chunk arrives, and not when a tool or subagent wait begins (that request is over).
  Compaction enters the same pool with `purpose: 'compaction'`, and every official retry takes a
  fresh permit. The guard is open only while a restore runs, so ordinary chatting is never queued
  behind it.

The pool starts at `restoreCapacity` (1). Two clean streams in a row raise it by one, up to
`restoreMaxCapacity` (2). Two failures in a row drop it back to one and close the pool for
`restoreCooldownMs` (40 s), so one unwell upstream cannot be hammered by a queue of sessions. An
abandoned stream (the person paused) is neither a success nor a strike: cancelling is cheap.

The switch is read when you press restore; a running batch keeps the setting it started with, so
turning the feature off mid-batch cannot suddenly release the queue. Press pause to stop the
current batch.

Nothing about reliability depends on this switch. Pause and restore of sessions, subagents and
background jobs, pausing again during a restore, plan persistence, crash recovery, continuation
deduplication and the retry entry all still apply with progressive restore off. The restore loop
keeps its own small worker waves either way; only the extra limit on real model requests is
optional.

Pausing while a restore is running is immediate. The press stops dispatching, refuses every request
still waiting for a permit, asks the Harness to stop the work that already started, writes what is
left back to the plan as an outstanding continuation, and returns `paused` with
`interrupted: true`. The next press resumes the same plan; the continuation request id is per cycle,
so a message already admitted is deduplicated instead of sent twice.

`/state` reports the setting and the queue while a plan exists: `{progressive, active, enabled,
capacity, running, queued, dispatched, failed, interrupted, cooldownUntil}` under `restore`. The
button itself stays icon-only.

Configuration (all optional):

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `restoreProgressive` | `false` | opt-in staged restore; off keeps the plain path |
| `restoreCapacity` | `1` | model requests allowed when a restore starts |
| `restoreMaxCapacity` | `2` | ceiling the health gate may raise the limit to |
| `restoreCooldownMs` | `40000` | pause after two consecutive failures across sessions |
| `restoreStartGapMs` | `3000` | spacing between restore starts, plus jitter |
| `wrapUpMs` | `3000` | how long a running turn has to wrap up before a pause cancels it |

Scope, stated honestly: this governs requests that pass through this Host's model stack. The
Harness's own restore flow and a subagent that reaches a provider outside this Host are outside the
pool, and no plugin can promise a concurrency limit for a company gateway it does not own. The
300 s upstream idle timeout is an upstream decision; progressive restore cannot pretend to fix it,
but it makes the restore produce evidence (one session, one exact request) instead of an avalanche.

Restoring a session deserialises its whole transcript into the Host heap. One large session is
GB-scale on its own, and the Host's V8 has roughly a 4 GB ceiling; past it the process does not
throw, it dies with `FATAL ERROR: MarkCompactCollector: young object promotion failed`. Measured
twice on 2026-10-29: pid 91126 after 64 minutes at 3.65 GB, and pid 61989 fifteen minutes after
restoring 15 sessions at 3.58 GB. Both left `crash-*-host.log` under
`~/Library/Logs/DeepSeek Harness/`.
So a restore is paced by what it can afford to hold, not only by what it has to do:

* **Only what this crash interrupted.** Sessions recorded by the crash plan are restored; history
  and sessions that ended normally are never touched. That is unchanged since 0.6.x.
* **Smallest first.** The queue is ordered by transcript size, so light sessions go first and heavy
  ones last. Light sessions run `restoreConcurrency` (2) at a time.
* **Heavy sessions run alone.** A session whose compressed transcript is above `restoreHeavyMB`
  gets a step of its own; the next one starts when its turn ends, or after `restoreSettleMs` (90 s)
  as the upper bound.
* **One press drains the queue.** A row held back only because an earlier restored session was
  still working is retried by the engine itself, one `restoreSettleMs` later, until nothing is left.
  Before 0.8.4 the same press mounted exactly one large transcript and left the rest for a person to
  press for again, which is what `partial` after every restart looked like. The retry stops on a
  stop the person asked for, on a reload, and after `restoreMaxAttempts` rounds that restored
  nothing.
* **Heap gate.** Before each step the restore reads `v8.getHeapStatistics()`. If the headroom left
  is below `restoreHeapReserveMB`

A round that held rows back does not consume the plan: it ends `partial`, keeps every row on disk
with its `deferred` note, and `/state.restore.deferred` lists what it could not mount. Consuming it
would have deleted the only record of work that had never started, and the next boot would offer a
clean restore while a large session was still owed.

When a round restored a heavy session or produced `deferred`, `/state` also carries
`restartRecommended` with the heap usage and the reason, and the client's tooltip switches to
"重启后继续没放下的内容" once rows are waiting on a restart. The plugin never exits or restarts the Host itself: a process
is a person's running work, and a plugin that killed it for a cleaner heap would be paying with
data it does not own.

The advice lives as long as the work it is about: it is kept while `/state.scheduling.deferred`
lists rows that this round held back (the next press cannot mount them either), it is cleared by a
healthy round with nothing deferred, and a recommendation from more than six hours ago is dropped
unless rows are still waiting. A row that was held back keeps the intention it had (mount or
continue) and comes back with it on the next restore.

The three memory numbers are derived from the heap this Host actually has, not written down here:
a 4 GB V8 cap and a 16 GB one cannot share a reserve, and a small cap wants one session at a time.
`/state.scheduling` reports the resolved values plus `derived`, which says which of them came from
the heap instead of from config.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `restoreConcurrency` | `1` if the V8 cap is under 3 GB, else `2` | light sessions restored at once in one round |
| `restoreHeavyMB` | `heapLimitMB / 340`, clamped to 8–48 MB | compressed-transcript size that makes a session heavy |
| `restoreHeapReserveMB` | `22%` of the V8 cap, clamped to 320–1536 MB | heap headroom below which a round mounts nothing |
| `restoreSettleMs` | `90000` | upper bound to wait for a heavy session's turn |
| `restoreMaxAgeHours` | `72` | a crash record older than this is archived, not mounted |
All four are optional; setting one pins that number and leaves the others derived.

This is a different layer from progressive restore. `restoreProgressive`, `restoreCapacity`,
`restoreMaxCapacity` and `restoreCooldownMs` limit real model requests to the upstream; these four
limit how much transcript a restore holds and how many sessions it steps through. Both can be on,
and neither replaces the other. The crash evidence, the scheduling flow and the `deferred` /
`restartRecommended` fields are described in `docs/memory-safety.md`.

macOS, Windows and Linux. State and logs go through `node:path` and `node:fs` only, under
`$DSH_HOME` (or `~/.dsh` when the variable is unset); nothing calls a shell and nothing shells out
to `stat`, `du` or `ps`. Cross-process exclusion uses a `session.lock` file rather than POSIX-only
calls. On Windows the directory `fsync` has no equivalent, so it is skipped — a write is still a
temp file plus `rename` — and that, together with line endings, is the only difference between the
platforms.

```bash
plugin_manager install_bundle dsh-pause-resume
```

or install the bundle from the Harness plugin manager with the package name. Every configuration
key is optional (see Progressive restore) and the plugin holds no credentials. `allowRemote` exists for a Harness reached from another
machine; local-only is the default.

* **Exclusive.** The phase lives on the Host and is written before any work starts, so two windows,
  a double press and a tool call cannot overlap. The second caller is told `busy` — except a pause
  during a restore, which interrupts it on the spot instead of refusing: stopping must never be the
  operation that waits.
* **Durable before destructive.** No turn is cancelled until the plan is on disk. A failed write means
  nothing was stopped.
* **Bounded.** A restore that keeps failing stays on disk with its rows named; it does not close as
  if the work were finished. A row that cannot be read is retried once and then either reports real
  progress or retires the plan as `partial` with per-row attention, so the button stops repeating a
  no-op. Sessions continued by hand are restored, never re-sent, and their attention row clears as
  soon as they run. An attempt that overruns its budget is watched a little longer before it is
  called a failure, and a session this plan already restored stays restored even if the Harness
  revives it and moves its turn on a later boot.
* **Idempotent.** The continuation request id is derived from the plan and the session, so a retry
  cannot pos

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `snapshot.json` | the work a press stopped, `pausing` or `paused` |
| `pending.json` | a crash plan, kept until a restore finishes |
| `journal/<planId>.jsonl` | restore attempts, tagged with the boot that made them |
| `restores/<planId>.json` | the archived plan, kept as a record of the last restore |
| `last-restore.json` | summary of the last restore |
| `running.json` | sessions with an open turn, for crash residue |
| `continue.json` | turns that stopped on their own and wait for one continue press |

Every write is a unique temp file, `fsync`, `rename`, then a directory `fsync`. State is never inside
the package.

The wrap-up path has its own record in `docs/evidence/host-wrapup.json` (a real turn that ends itself
inside the window, so the plan owes one continuation), next to `docs/evidence/host-live.json` (a
window that expires, where the press takes its own steer back).

Verification records live in `docs/acceptance-0.6.11.md` (current release: repeated failures stay
continuable, a pause truncates a running batch, admission ownership, handoff proof, cold/stale goal
recovery, continue behind the progressive gate, and blocking vs actionable rows, with the proven and
unproven halves kept apart), `docs/acceptance-0.6.10.md` (self-stopped turns and the one continue press), `docs/acceptance-0.6.9.md` (the ten defects from the previous review), `docs/acceptance-0.6.7.md` (a crash press that moved the
button without restarting anything), `docs/acceptance-0.6.6.md` (an `unknown` row a person

`lib/engine.js` performs no I/O, `lib/snapshot.js` persists, `lib/probe.js` holds every Harness service
contract (agent identity, goal revision, per-owner jobs, continuation prompts), and `index.js` only
wires them to the web routes. All of them are testable without a Harness: `test/apply.test.mjs` mounts
the plugin against a fake registry.

一行说明：会话头一个按钮，⏸ 停掉正在跑的回合、目标与后台任务；重启后同一个按钮变 ▶，把上次的工作
接回来。正常结束的会话不记录、不恢复；崩溃会接回记录里的会话与其目标，暂时无法确认状态的会话保持计划未完成，按钮继续给 ▶；日程不会被动
（该服务只有删除，没有停用），后台命令只记录不重跑。
